adr_markdown:
# ADR: Modular Monolith with Internal Evented Projections and CQRS

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The system must support rider and administrator experiences for a bike-rental platform while meeting security, privacy, compliance, reporting, and responsiveness needs. The selected architecture must handle authenticated access, verification and payment flows, rental lifecycle management, bike availability updates, and historical reporting without introducing unnecessary operational complexity.

The decision also needs to balance cross-channel access, centralized consistency for rental and billing workflows, and timely read access for discovery and reporting. The evaluated options show a spectrum from a simple modular monolith to a fully distributed microservices architecture. The chosen approach should preserve deployment simplicity while still improving freshness of rider and administrator views.

## Decision

Adopt alternative A3: a modular monolith organized with hexagonal boundaries, internal event publication, CQRS-style read models, and internal process coordination for rental and payment workflows.

This decision keeps the system as a single deployable application with clear business modules and isolated adapters, while using internal events and specialized projections to improve discovery, availability, and reporting reads. Core transactional workflows remain centralized within the application boundary.

## Rationale

A3 was selected because it satisfies all stated requirements while offering the best overall balance of simplicity, freshness of reads, and operational prudence.

From the evaluation, A3 meets the functional requirements for registration, authentication, rental management, payment handling, timeout behavior, history retention, and administrative reporting. It also aligns well with the major architectural drivers: security and privacy, cross-channel access, user experience simplicity, time-sensitive rider interactions, and operational reporting.

Compared with A1, A3 improves rider and administrator view freshness by introducing internal evented projections, while still retaining the single deployable boundary and centralized consistency advantages of a monolith. Compared with A2, it avoids the higher complexity, heavier operational burden, and stronger consistency trade-offs of a distributed system.

The trade-off analysis shows that A3 is a pragmatic middle ground: it improves responsiveness and reporting without paying the full cost of microservices. The main remaining compromises are projection complexity and the fact that scalability and fault isolation are still bounded by a single application runtime.

## Alternatives Considered

### A1 - Modular Monolith with Hexagonal Architecture, API Gateway, and Saga / Process Manager

A1 proposed a single deployable modular application with hexagonal boundaries, an API gateway, and centralized workflow coordination.
It was not selected because, although it is strong on simplicity and consistency, it provides weaker freshness for discovery and reporting than A3. The evaluation and trade-off analysis indicate that A3 better serves time-sensitive rider interactions and administrative views through internal event-driven projections.

### A2 - Distributed Microservices with Event-Driven Integration

A2 proposed a set of independently deployable services with asynchronous integration and stronger fault isolation.
It was not selected because it introduces the highest architectural and operational complexity and weakens consistency relative to the other options. The evaluation highlights that the platform does not need microservices-level distribution to satisfy its requirements, and the trade-off analysis shows the added coordination, monitoring, and testing burden would be disproportionate.

## Consequences

### Positive Consequences

- Preserves the simplicity of a single deployable application.
- Maintains strong transactional consistency for rental and billing workflows.
- Improves rider discovery and administrator reporting through fresher read models.
- Supports security and compliance through clear internal boundaries and isolated adapters.
- Provides a pragmatic architecture that can evolve further if demand increases.

### Negative Consequences

- The system still has less fault isolation and elastic scaling than a distributed architecture.
- Internal event publication and projection maintenance add design and testing complexity.
- Read models can become temporarily stale if projection processing lags.
- A monolith-wide runtime failure can impact many user flows at once.
- Future growth may require later service extraction, creating migration cost.

## Traceability

- Requirements: S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S6, S7, S8, S9, S10, S11, S12, S13
- Quality attributes: security and privacy, usability, availability, performance and responsiveness, data consistency, interoperability, localization and regulatory compliance
- Architectural drivers: security, privacy, and regulatory compliance; cross-channel access for riders and administrators; user experience simplicity; time-sensitive rider interactions; operational reporting and history retention
